lead: A linear time-invariant system is BIBO stable when every bounded input produces a bounded output. This is decided by the poles of the closed-loop transfer function. If every pole lies strictly inside the left half of the s-plane, all natural modes decay. If any pole sits on the jω axis or to its right, some bounded input drives the output to infinity. Every stability test in this unit locates those poles without factorising the denominator.
prereq: Unit 1 for transfer functions, poles, zeros and block diagrams; Unit 2 for step and ramp inputs.

blocks.text: Take input u(t) and output y(t). An input is bounded when a finite number M exists with |u(t)| ≤ M for all t ≥ 0. An output is bounded the same way, with some finite N. The system is BIBO stable when every bounded input produces a bounded output.
For an LTI system with impulse response h(t), the test is ∫₀^∞ |h(t)| dt < ∞. For a rational transfer function this becomes a pole condition.

blocks.where: T(s) is the closed-loop transfer function; G(s) is the forward-path transfer function; H(s) is the feedback-path transfer function; G(s)H(s) is the loop gain. For unity feedback H(s) = 1 and T(s) = G(s)/(1 + G(s)).

blocks.text: BIBO stability is a property of the input–output pair only. It says nothing about the internal states of the system.
Write T(s) = N(s)/D(s) with all fractions cleared. D(s) is the characteristic polynomial and D(s) = 0 the characteristic equation. In general the characteristic equation is:

blocks.where: G(s) is the forward path and H(s) the feedback path; with H(s) = 1 it becomes 1 + G(s) = 0. After clearing fractions this is a polynomial in s whose roots are the closed-loop poles.

blocks.text: Poles are values of s where T(s) becomes infinite: roots of D(s). Zeros are values where T(s) = 0: roots of N(s). A transfer function with n poles and m zeros has n − m zeros at infinity when n > m. Every pole is real or one of a complex-conjugate pair, because coefficients are real.

A pole–zero plot marks poles as × and zeros as ○ on the complex s-plane. The horizontal axis is σ, the real part. The vertical axis is jω, the imaginary part, and is the boundary between left and right half-planes.
Partial fractions turn each pole p = σ + jω into a term K e<sup>pt</sup>, where K is set by the residues.
e<sup>pt</sup> = e<sup>σt</sup>(cos ωt + j sin ωt)
blocks.where: σ is the real part of the pole, in per second; it sets growth or decay. ω is the imaginary part, in rad/s; it sets oscillation frequency.

items: Negative real part, open left half-plane: e<sup>σt</sup> decays, so the response settles. BIBO stable.
Zero real part, on the jω axis: constant-amplitude oscillation. Called marginally stable, and limitedly stable in some syllabi.
Positive real part, open right half-plane: e<sup>σt</sup> grows without limit. Unstable.

blocks.text: A simple pole at s = 0 gives a constant impulse response, but a step input is 1/s, so the pole at the origin appears twice and the output contains a t term that grows without limit. The case that survives a step is a simple pair at s = ±jω₀: the step response is a bounded oscillation, but an input sin ω₀t makes those poles double and the response grows. A repeated pole at the origin gives t even for an impulse. So a simple jω pair is only marginally stable; repeated jω poles are unstable. The closed-loop pole or pair closest to the jω axis decides settling speed, as dominant poles explains.

Feedback shifts the closed-loop poles away from the open-loop poles. Take G(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)) with unity feedback. The open-loop poles are 0 and −2, so the open loop is only marginally stable; its impulse response does not decay. The characteristic equation is s² + 2s + 1 = 0, a double pole at −1: the closed loop is stable.

The reverse happens too. G(s) = 100/((s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3)) is open-loop stable, with poles at −1, −2 and −3. Unity feedback gives s³ + 6s² + 11s + 106 = 0, whose roots include a pair in the right half-plane; Unit 4 reaches the same conclusion from the Nyquist plot. Testing the poles of G(s) alone is therefore a mistake.

Asymptotic stability demands more: every mode must decay, including modes that a zero cancels. A pole cancelled by a zero never appears in T(s), so the input–output test cannot see it. Checking it needs the state model of Unit 6; only a few universities teach that distinction at this stage. Use the Routh–Hurwitz criterion when the polynomial is too large to factorise.

figure.caption: A pole at −1 gives a decaying exponential, a pole at 0 gives a flat line, and a pole at +0.5 grows without limit. Only the left-half pole settles.

spec.aria: Three curves against time: a decaying exponential for a pole at s = −1, a flat line at 1 for a pole at s = 0, and a growing exponential for a pole at s = +0.5.

examples.question: T(s) = (s + 5)/((s + 3)(s² + 2s + 5)). (a) List poles and zeros. (b) Decide BIBO stability. (c) Find the steady value of its unit-step response. (d) Repeat (b) for T(s) = (s + 5)/((s − 1)(s² + 2s + 5)).
steps: All real parts are −3, −1, −1, all negative, so every mode decays and the system is BIBO stable.
Final value: T(0) = 5/(3 × 5) = 1/3 = 0.333 of the step size.
Part (d): s − 1 gives a pole at +1. Its mode e<sup>t</sup> grows without bound; no final value exists and the system is unstable.
examples.answer: Poles −3 and −1 ± j2; zero −5; first system BIBO stable with c(∞) = 0.333; second unstable, no steady value.
examples.check:
import math
a, b, c = 1.0, 2.0, 5.0
disc = b*b - 4*a*c
re = -b/(2*a)
im = math.sqrt(-disc)/(2*a)
print(-5.0)
print(-3.0)
print(re)
print(im)
print(-im)
print(round(5.0/((0+3)*(0+0+5)), 3))

traps: Testing the poles of G(s) instead of the roots of 1 + G(s)H(s). The plant 100/((s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3)) is open-loop stable, yet the closed loop is unstable.

Calling a pole on the jω axis stable. A simple pair at s = ±j2 passes a step input but fails a sine at 2 rad/s, which makes the pair double and gives t·sin 2t. A simple pole at s = 0 fails even a step input: the step doubles the origin pole and the output is a ramp.
Sign slip: the root of s + 3 = 0 is s = −3, not +3. Solve the factor; do not read off the constant.
Forgetting that repeated jω poles grow. A factor (s² + 4)² contributes t·sin 2t, not a bounded oscillation.
Assuming a cancelled pole–zero pair has vanished. It disappears from T(s) only; the mode still lives inside the system.

quiz.q: State the BIBO stability condition on the poles of a closed-loop transfer function.
quiz.a: Every pole must lie strictly in the open left half of the s-plane, so every pole has a negative real part.

quiz.q: Write the characteristic equation for a unity-feedback system with forward transfer function G(s).
quiz.a: 1 + G(s) = 0, cleared of fractions; its roots are the closed-loop poles.

quiz.q: A system has simple poles at s = ±j2. Its unit-step response is a bounded oscillation. Why is it still not BIBO stable?
quiz.a: The step input has its own pole at s = 0, which does not coincide with ±j2, so no resonance occurs. An input sin 2t adds poles at ±j2; those poles become double and the partial fractions carry a t·sin 2t term that grows without limit. BIBO stability needs every bounded input to give a bounded output, so one counterexample is enough. (A simple pole at s = 0 is worse: it fails even a step input, giving a ramp.)

quiz.q: A pole–zero pair at s = −2 cancels in T(s). What does BIBO stability say, and what does it miss?
quiz.a: T(s) hides the cancelled pole, so BIBO stability sees only the remaining poles. The mode e<sup>−2t</sup> still exists inside the system; internal stability, checked with the state model, is stronger.

quiz.q: For T(s) = 10/((s + 2)(s² + 4)), list the poles and decide BIBO stability.
quiz.a: Poles: s = −2 and s = ±j2. The jω pair gives sustained oscillation at 2 rad/s. Not all real parts are negative, so the system is not BIBO stable; it is marginally stable.

quiz.q: For T(s) = (s + 1)/(s² + 3s + 2), find the poles, the zeros, the stability and the unit-step final value.
quiz.a: s² + 3s + 2 = (s + 1)(s + 2), so poles are −1 and −2; zero at −1. Both real parts negative, so BIBO stable. Final value T(0) = 1/2 = 0.5.

quiz.q: G(s) = 100/((s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3)) with unity feedback. The open loop is stable. Is the closed loop?
quiz.a: Characteristic equation: (s + 1)(s + 2)(s + 3) + 100 = s³ + 6s² + 11s + 106 = 0. The first column is 1, 6, −6.67, 106, with two sign changes, so two roots lie in the right half-plane. The closed loop is unstable.

quiz.q: Why is a pole on the jω axis dangerous even when the step response looks bounded?
quiz.a: The step response is bounded only because the step pole at 0 does not coincide with ±jω₀. A sinusoid at ω₀ makes the jω pair double; the response contains a t·sin ω₀t term and grows without limit, so BIBO fails. A simple pole at s = 0 fails even a step, giving a ramp.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real plants drift, and robust stability asks whether the loop stays stable for every plant in a family. The s-plane picture becomes the Nyquist criterion; the same poles become eigenvalues of the A matrix in state space. Search for internal stability and H-infinity robust stability next.
